description: NCS is a nonprofit in Londrina, Brazil. Our project, Radar do Bairro, uses NISAR radar and explainable ML to detect floods and land change in low-income neighborhoods, then crosses it with census data to show who is affected. After the hackathon it becomes a real community program. I’m a computational chemist (Python). Looking for: ML, SAR/remote sensing, GIS/web maps, design and storytelling. Beginners welcome! PT/EN.
summary: Neighborhood Radar asks a simple question: after heavy rain, does NASA–ISRO’s NISAR radar see changes where the terrain says water tends to go? We built four open Python notebooks and an interactive web map for São Lourenço, a neighborhood in Londrina, Brazil. They compare eight NISAR L-band radar passes (June–October 2026) with daily rain from NASA’s GPM IMERG and water-flow paths computed from the Copernicus elevation model. A dry-date control and a spatial randomization test tell us how much to trust each result. The radar clearly senses rain: the share of 100 m blocks that turned strongly brighter grew from 0.5% on a dry date to 5.0% after 79 mm. But the brightening was spread across yards, lots and green edges, not concentrated where water collects, which points to wet soil and plants rather than standing water. This matters because it shows, with honest checks, what a new free satellite can and cannot tell a community about rain. Residents, schools and local government can click any block to see its radar “rhythm” next to the rain, and anyone can rerun the notebooks for another neighborhood.
details:
What it does and how it works

Neighborhood Radar tests whether NASA–ISRO’s NISAR radar can show how a neighborhood responds to rain. The study area is a 3 km × 3 km square in São Lourenço, Londrina, Brazil, a mix of dense housing, open lots and green valleys. The workflow has four open Jupyter notebooks that run in Google Colab:

  1. Radar (01). Downloads eight NISAR L2 GCOV scenes (L-band, 20 m, track 053 descending, June–October 2026) from the ASF DAAC and crops the study area. For each rainy date, it computes the change in dB against the average of three dry dates. A dry control built the same way (three dry dates against a fourth) sets what “normal” change looks like. A check on stable targets (buildings) separates real change from scene-wide calibration offsets.
  2. Terrain (02). Places the Copernicus DEM on the same 20 m grid, fills depressions, routes flow downhill (D8) and computes the height above the nearest drainage (HAND). The lowest 20% of HAND marks where water tends to go.
  3. Concordance (03). Tests whether strong radar change falls inside those zones more than chance. It removes the scene median, uses thresholds taken from the dry control, runs 999 circular shifts of the terrain map (keeping its spatial pattern) and applies false discovery rate correction.
  4. Page (04). Builds a static website from the results files, with no number typed by hand. It has an interactive satellite map, a date selector and a “rhythm of the place” chart: click any 100 m block to see its radar signal on all eight dates next to the rain.

Daily rain from NASA’s GPM IMERG (via Giovanni) was used to choose the dates and to describe each pass.

What we found

The radar senses rain. The share of 100 m blocks that turned strongly brighter grew with the rain of the 3 days before each pass:

  • 0.5% on a dry date;
  • 1.1% (23.5 mm);
  • 2.5% (31.4 mm);
  • 5.0% (79.2 mm).

The brightening was spread across yards, lots and green edges, not concentrated where water tends to collect: none of the 24 tests on rainy dates was significant, and the dry control gave no false alarms. This points to wet soil and vegetation, and to fast urban drainage, rather than standing water. An exploratory analysis, decided after seeing the data, found slightly more change at low HAND on Jul 23 (rho −0.08 HH, −0.07 HV, p = 0.10). It is reported as a lead, not a result.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It shows, with honest checks, what a new free satellite can and cannot tell a community about rain, before anyone relies on it.
  • Residents, schools and local government can explore their own neighborhood on a map that works in any browser without login.
  • NCS, a non-profit in Londrina, will use it in education activities on space data, climate and the city.
  • Anyone can rerun it for another place by changing the area and dates in one configuration cell.
  • Every notebook saves its results as open files (GeoTIFF, PNG, JSON with units), ready for other researchers or AI tools.

Tools

  • Python in Jupyter notebooks on Google Colab: asf_search, h5py, numpy, scipy, rasterio, pyproj, matplotlib.
  • Leaflet and Plotly for the web page, published with GitHub Pages.
  • NASA Earthdata, ASF Vertex and NASA Giovanni.
  • No special hardware.

Creative aspects

  • It uses data from a mission that is only a few months old, applied to a working-class urban neighborhood rather than a large river flood.
  • It joins radar, rain and terrain on one grid and turns a technical test into a map anyone can click.
  • The “rhythm of the place” view lets people see their street’s radar signal rise and fall with the rain.
  • It treats a negative result as a finding worth showing.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty. Dry control, calibration check, spatial test and multiple-testing correction, with exploratory results labeled as such.
  • Limitations stated on the page. One area, one radar geometry, few rain events, 20–100 m pixels, a surface model that sees roofs and not drains, rain at about 10 km resolution, and HV not corrected for noise.
  • Not a warning system. It is a science and education tool, and the page says so.
  • Open and safe. MIT license, all data sources credited, no login data stored in the code, and no images of people.
  • Use of AI is disclosed in the notebooks and on the page.
